steps.say: Some children are left with too little working gut to grow, either because dead bowel was removed or the remaining bowel cannot absorb. The commonest roads to this state are severe bowel infection of prematurity, sealed bowel at birth, exposed bowel from a wall defect, and a midgut twist. About one baby in three here arrives after necrotising infection.
steps.tx: **Short bowel syndrome** (gut failure) means inadequate absorption for growth from massive resection or dysfunction, with an **etiology** (cause mix) led by **necrotising enterocolitis** (premature gut infection) at **35** (thirty five) percent, atresia at **25** (twenty five) percent, **gastroschisis** (exposed bowel) at **18** (eighteen) percent and **midgut volvulus** (whole-bowel twist) at **14** (fourteen) percent.

steps.say: How the child fares depends on plumbing more than on any drug. Healthy remaining lining, enough length, a narrow calibre, the valve at the end, which segments survive, and whether germs stagnate all decide. Thirty five to forty centimetres gives a coin-flip chance of leaving drip feeds, with four percent added for every extra centimetre.
steps.tx: Function depends on villous **architecture** (lining health), length, diameter, **ileocecal valve** (end valve), residual segments, stasis and **bacterial overgrowth** (germ stagnation), with **35** (thirty five) to **40** (forty) cm giving a **50** (fifty) percent chance of **enteral autonomy** (drip-free feeding) off **parenteral nutrition** (vein feeds) plus **4** (four) percent per extra centimeter.

steps.say: Each segment of bowel has its own special cargo. The upper small bowel takes most nutrients and minerals, while the last stretch handles complex sugars, fluids, salts, bile acids and the vitamins that need bile for uptake. Losing the tail end costs the child B twelve and the fat-soluble vitamins.
steps.tx: **Jejunum** (upper small bowel) absorbs most macronutrients and minerals while **ileum** (lower small bowel) handles carbohydrates, proteins, fluids, electrolytes, **bile acids** (fat-digesting salts), vitamin **B12** (nerve vitamin) and fat soluble vitamins **A** (A), **D** (D), **E** (E) and **K** (K).

steps.say: Milk is medicine in this disease. Human milk composition with its changing stages outperforms cow milk for the fragile gut, and the comparison table shows why protein and fat content alone never tell the story. Feeds advance drop by drop while the drip still covers growth, transitioning slowly.
steps.tx: Enteral **nutrition** (gut feeding) with **breast milk** (human milk) outperforms formula for the adapting gut, and the milk comparison table guides protein, fat and stage choices. **Continuous feeds** (slow drip feeds) suit a stressed gut before transition to **bolus feeds** (meal feeds) as tolerance grows.

steps.say: The remaining bowel is not static; it grows wider and taller to compensate if it is fed. The end of the small bowel adapts best of all, which is probably what the famous valve really marks. The colon pitches in by reclaiming water and salts after massive loss upstream.
steps.tx: The terminal **ileum** (end segment) adapts best so the valve likely just marks its presence, and the **colon** (large bowel) importantly reclaims water and **electrolytes** (salts) after massive resection. **Intestinal adaptation** (compensatory growth) is aided by **elemental diet** (predigested feeds), **growth factors** (gut hormones) and titrated parenteral support.

steps.say: Old operations that slowed the gut with reversed segments, recycling loops, artificial valves and pacemakers all failed and were abandoned. They traded obstruction and germ overgrowth for a little extra transit time. Modern care lengthens the bowel itself instead, abandoning old tricks. Zinc, selenium and the fat-soluble vitamins are replaced by protocol.
steps.tx: Old transit slowing tricks like **reversed segments** (backwards loops), recirculating loops, valves, **colon interposition** (colon bridge) and pacing failed and were abandoned. They caused **obstruction** (blockage) and **bacterial overgrowth** (germ excess) without durable weaning from parenteral support. Zinc, selenium and **fat soluble vitamins** (A, D, E, K) are replaced by protocol.

steps.say: Severe wasting shows what is at stake when absorption fails. The swollen child with pale hair and the skeletal child with loose skin folds are two faces of the same protein-energy gap. Preventing this picture is the entire point of intestinal rehabilitation.
steps.tx: **Malnutrition** (nutrient gap) in gut failure spans **kwashiorkor** (swollen protein deficiency) and **marasmus** (skeletal energy deficiency), tracked by weight, arm circumference and growth charts. **Multidisciplinary intestinal rehabilitation** (team gut-failure care) governs selection and follow up, since surgery alone never replaces nutritional management.

vis.alt: Side-by-side illustration of kwashiorkor and marasmus in paediatric severe malnutrition.
vis.caption: Kwashiorkor versus marasmus: the stakes of intestinal failure. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Two lengthening operations dominate modern practice. One splits the stretched bowel lengthwise into two leaves joined end to end, halving width and doubling length at the cost of vascular risk. The other staples alternating Vs across the bowel, easier and repeatable, with roughly half the children reaching feed independence in the reported series.
steps.tx: The **Bianchi procedure** (longitudinal lengthening) splits dilated bowel on two **mesenteric leaves** (blood-supply sheets) and joins ends in series, halving diameter and doubling length (**100** (one hundred) percent gain), **Serial transverse enteroplasty** (stapled V lengthening) narrows and lengthens more simply, and a **36** (thirty six) patient review showed **53** (fifty three) percent length gain with **42** (forty two) percent reaching **enteral autonomy** (feed independence). **Multidisciplinary intestinal rehabilitation** (team gut-failure care) governs **patient selection** (candidate choice), the core of **multidisciplinary care** (team management).
